title: Motion to Intervene and Comments of Data Center Coalition on Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.’s proposal to establish the Large Load Additional Resource Study framework under ER27-25.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                       )
Midcontinent Independent System                        )                      Docket No. ER27-25-000
Operator, Inc.                                         )

                            MOTION TO INTERVENE
                  AND COMMENTS OF THE DATA CENTER COALITION

        Pursuant to Rules 211, 212, and 214 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”) 1 and the Commission’s October

2, 2026 Combined Notice of Filings #1, 2 the Data Center Coalition (“DCC”) hereby moves to

intervene and submits these comments on Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.’s

(“MISO”) proposal to establish the Large Load Additional Resource Study (LARS) framework 3

I.      INTRODUCTION

        DCC is the membership organization for the U.S. data center industry, representing

leading data center owners and operators that develop, operate, and maintain data center

infrastructure and teams across the country. 4 DCC members operate data centers that constitute

significant loads within the MISO region and DCC has been an active stakeholder in regional

efforts to ensure reliability, enable new generation, and discipline load forecasts. DCC and its

members have been at the forefront of efforts to advance reforms to accommodate the growth of

 large loads within the MISO region while maintaining reliability and protecting existing retail

customers.

        As the industry unlocks unprecedented economic opportunities across the country and in

the MISO region, supporting affordability is a foundational priority for DCC members and the

communities they serve. DCC advocates for grid reforms that minimize unnecessary cost

burdens, align with cost causation principles, facilitate responsible load growth, support the

development of new generation, and enhance grid resilience system-wide without imposing

undue costs on existing ratepayers. DCC members are committed to supporting the generation

and infrastructure additions required to serve their demand responsibly.

        DCC commends MISO’s proactive engagement with stakeholders and the data center

community to develop innovative study process reforms to facilitate the timely integration of

large loads while maintaining system reliability and affordability. DCC member facilities depend

upon reliable and cost-effective electricity service, and DCC shares MISO’s objective of

ensuring that the interconnection and operation of large load customers does not adversely affect

reliability, system operations, or other transmission customers. Accordingly, DCC supports

MISO’s proposed LARS framework for the expedited, coordinated study of certain generation-

load pairs as a pragmatic new pathway to “facilitate the cost effective, timely and reliable

integration of new large loads into the system”5 by allowing large loads to support both the

generation as well as infrastructure additions required to serve their demand while also

addressing Commission directives in its June 18, 2026 Order to Show Cause. 6

        6

 II.    COMMENTS IN SUPPORT

       A. LARS Modernizes Transmission Service and Generator Interconnection Study
          Processes to Align with the Pace of Economic Growth
       DCC members are committed to supporting regional economic expansion as reliable grid

citizens, supporting reforms that facilitate responsible load growth and new generation

development while protecting ratepayer affordability and system resilience. MISO projects

annual load growth of 1% to 3% through 2044, driven by the expansion of energy-intensive

industries including data centers as well as advanced manufacturing. 7 Meeting the unprecedented

growth in MISO’s footprint responsibly and reliably requires a modernized approach to resource

integration and identification of grid upgrades and the LARS proposal embodies this necessary

evolution. The LARS proposal provides a productive and targeted framework for studying

qualifying large loads (200 MW or greater) alongside contractually paired new generation in the

same Local Resource Zone (“LRZ”) on an expedited 120-day cycle. By evaluating this group of

load and generation pairs on a coordinated and concurrent basis, LARS offers a practical tool

that will bring essential supply online quickly to support MISO’s economic growth while

optimizing network upgrades and protecting overall customer affordability. Such an approach is

directly aligned with DCC’s objective of ensuring data centers and other large load customers

take appropriate responsibility for supporting the development of new generation and

infrastructure necessary to serve their demand.

       For generation and load that are contractually associated, the traditional approach of

disaggregated generation queue and transmission service study processes can result in inaccurate

study results and unnecessary delays that fail to match the pace of economic growth and need for




       7
           Filing, Transmittal Letter at 2.

                                                  3
 new supply. Failing to reflect contractually associated generators when studying the provision of

transmission service for large loads can create an incomplete and inaccurate picture of grid

conditions. This may lead to the identification of inefficient, unnecessary, or costly Network

Upgrades that do not match actual grid impacts.

         In response to these challenges, MISO’s LARS framework provides a new pathway

offering load customers new optionality to access a coordinated and expedited study pathway for

the discrete set of circumstances where eligible large loads have contractually associated

generation located in the same LRZ. By studying this discrete set of load-generation pairs

concurrently under LARS, MISO will be able to produce a more realistic picture of the grid,

creating opportunities for MISO to potentially optimize Network Upgrades. Additionally, the

more streamlined 120-day process proposed under the LARS framework can bring both needed

supply and demand online efficiently, aligning with the original federal objectives of the

Department of Energy’s (DOE) Speed to Power Initiative to accelerate development timelines

for large-scale transmission and generation projects to meet rising electricity demand. 8

         B. LARS Supports Ratepayer Affordability By Facilitating New Generation,
            Optimizing Network Upgrades, and Isolating Network Upgrade Costs

         As the industry unlocks unprecedented economic opportunities across the country and in

the MISO footprint, supporting affordability is a priority for DCC members and the communities

they serve. DCC acknowledges that bringing significant new large loads online without enabling

sufficient new generation supply may exacerbate tight grid conditions and resource adequacy

concerns, putting upward pressure on prices or inappropriately shift costs to existing ratepayers.




         8
           U.S. Department of Energy’s Speed to Power Initiative (Sept. 18, 2025). See also, Filing, Transmittal
Letter at 2.

                                                         4
 The DCC will continue to champion reforms that enable data centers to bring their own

generation capacity as a method to insulate existing ratepayers from the costs of serving demand

from large load customers. The LARS framework is an example of such a reform. LARS can

mitigate cost risks by creating the opportunity for MISO to explore optimized transmission

solutions, offering a pathway that encourages large loads to proactively identify and bring new

generation supply to directly satisfy their new energy demands, and producing a more holistic

view of Network Upgrades that can be appropriately allocated under future cost allocation

reforms.

       First, LARS supports affordability by allowing MISO to more accurately evaluate the

impact of both load and generation on the transmission system, allowing MISO to consider

optimized configurations of Network Upgrades, potentially reducing unnecessary infrastructure

investment and associated costs. Moreover, the LARS framework can help provide cost

transparency by isolating the Network Upgrades needed to support these discrete generation-load

pairs, which can better inform cost allocation methods.

       Additionally, access to a coordinated and expedited 120-day study process creates an

incentive for new large load customers to proactively contract with new generation supply,

allowing large load customers to support the generation and infrastructure additions required to

serve their demand responsibly. DCC welcomes MISO’s balanced approach of introducing new

pathways and optionality, without mandating that new large loads must bring their own

generation.

       Finally, DCC also recognizes that the appropriate allocation of costs for transmission

upgrades identified through LARS, and other transmission service study processes, remains an

important issue to be addressed through MISO's ongoing stakeholder process. Any resulting cost

                                                5
 allocation framework should reflect cost causation, recognize benefits to the broader

transmission system, and avoid inappropriate cost shifts to existing customers. In alignment with

these principles, DCC members proudly joined over 200 governors, utilities, electric

cooperatives, and industry leaders in supporting the White House’s “Ratepayer Protection

Pledge.”9

III.    CONCERNS AND ROOM FOR IMPROVEMENT

        While DCC supports MISO’s LARS proposal as a productive framework that facilitates

the timely integration of large loads, DCC acknowledges outstanding concerns regarding access

to the generator interconnection queue under this process. Under MISO’s proposed framework,

all LARS applications must be submitted exclusively through the new “LARS Associated

Transmission Customer,”10 typically the Load-Serving Entity (“LSE”). As a result, third-party

generation owners cannot submit a LARS generator interconnection request directly to MISO

and must instead route requests through the LSE, restricting their direct participation and ability

to reap the benefits of the new expedited generator interconnection study under the LARS

framework.

        While it is appropriate for LSEs with obligations to serve load to manage load-side

requests under LARS, requiring all supporting generation to route through an LSE for purposes

of accessing a FERC-jurisdictional generator interconnection queue imposes unnecessary

restrictions. In MISO’s primarily vertically integrated footprint, establishing the LSE as the sole

LARS application facilitator narrows the pool of supply that can gain access to expedited Large




        9
           Ratepayer Protection Pledge, THE WHITE HOUSE, Proclamation No. 11014, 91 Fed. Reg. 11439 (Mar.
4, 2026), https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/. See also,
         10
            Filing, Transmittal Letter at P 7, see also id. at P 6 n. 23.

                                                    6
 Load Generation Interconnection Agreements (“LLGIAs”) to only those projects that are

effectively approved by the LSE. In contrast, most FERC-jurisdictional queue processes,

including MISO’s DPP and ERAS, allow all generators to directly submit interconnection

requests and execute interconnection agreements without LSE approval, aligned with FERC’s

open access principles. DCC clarifies that its concern strictly pertains to maximizing generator

access to expedited LLGIAs, while fully recognizing state jurisdictional authority over retail

service, including decisions regarding retail competition for generation.

       In response to these concerns, DCC supports approval of the proposed LARS framework,

but requests FERC encourage MISO to consider improvements for independent generator access,

such as allowing third-party generators with demonstrated commercial pairings to submit LARS

generator interconnect requests directly to MISO alongside the load application, or explore

additional transparency and evaluation metrics regarding LSE decisions on LARS application

selection. Broad access will expand the pool of supply that has access to expedited LLGIAs,

ultimately supporting new demand.

       Finally, following implementation experience with LARS, MISO could also consider

additional improvements to ensure program effectiveness, including whether greater flexibility in

the generation-to-load ratio and minimum generation project size would better support supply

diversification and resilience, as well as whether a more defined transition period could help

operating LARS loads maintain transmission service while securing replacement generation if

such instances arise.

IV.    MOTION TO INTERVENE

       DCC respectfully moves to intervene in this proceeding. DCC is the membership

organization for the U.S. data center industry, representing leading data center owners and

                                                 7
 operators that develop, operate, and maintain data center infrastructure and teams across the

country. DCC members operate data centers that constitute significant loads within the MISO

region and have been at the forefront of efforts to advance reforms to accommodate the growth

of large loads within the MISO region while maintaining reliability and protecting existing retail

customers.

       DCC’s member companies provide the essential digital infrastructure that underpins the

modern economy and supports critical public services, including cloud computing, artificial

intelligence, emergency response systems, and public safety operations. From 2017 to 2023, the

data center industry contributed $3.5 trillion to U.S. GDP. DCC advocates for grid reforms that

minimize unnecessary cost burdens, align with cost causation principles, facilitate responsible

load growth, support the development of new generation, and enhance grid resilience system-

wide without imposing undue costs on existing ratepayers.

       For the above reasons, DCC has a substantial interest in the outcome of this proceeding

that cannot be represented adequately by any other participant to this proceeding. DCC’s

intervention is in the public interest and its motion for leave to intervene in this proceeding

should be granted.
